title: Reduce prompt-side tokenization overhead via lexeme cache and single-pass parse pipeline
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: a disproportionate amount of CPU and tail latency on our hosted inference path is spent on prompt preprocessing (normalization, encoding, and tokenization) at the prefill stage. This issue is most visible for high QPS customers that reuse template prompts and for small/short prompts where tokenization dominates end-to-end latency.

Goal: design and land a lightweight tokenizer pipeline that: 1) avoids repeated work for commonly seen prompt fragments (system messages, templates, commons), 2) performs normalization + tokenization in a single pass to minimize memory churn, and 3) provides fast-paths for ASCII and small prompts. Expected outcome is measurable reduction in CPU spent on tokenization and an improvement to p95/p99 prefill latency while keeping correctness across model vocabularies and multibyte inputs.
acceptance_criteria: Reduce CPU cycles attributed to tokenization on the prefill path by >= 35% for our 3 high-volume tenants (measured on runtime-1.22 canary)
Improve prefill p95 latency for <128 char prompts by >= 20ms in the hosted baseline workload
No regression in tokenization correctness: roundtrip (text -> tokens -> detokenize) matches original text for 99.99% of sampled prompts including multibyte/unicode cases
Feature gated and configurable per-tenant (off by default for Private deployments until KMS/auditing checks pass)
End-to-end integration tests and fuzz tests added to the tokenization package; performance dashboards hooked into Console
implementation_plan: Spike: microbenchmarks to compare current tokenizer, single-pass UTF8-aware tokenizer, and a memcached lexeme memoization layer (2 days) — results recorded in the spike doc
Design: API contract for TokenizationPipeline with three pluggable stages: normalize, lexeme-cache-lookup, tokenize-on-miss
Engine: implement an in-process thread-safe LRU lexeme cache keyed by (model-vocab-hash, tenant-id, fragment-hash) with memory cap and per-model eviction policies
Fast-paths: ascii-only and short-prompt (<64 bytes) inline tokenizer implemented with SSE-friendly loops and no heap allocations
Scheduling: integrate with prefill/decode scheduler so frequent templates are pre-warmed and tokenized results can be reused across concurrent prefill requests
Tests: add deterministic tokenization tests, randomized unicode fuzzing, and perf harness recordings for CI
Canary rollout: runtime-1.22 canary with 5% traffic on hosted and dedicated preview for existing large tenants
Monitoring: add tokenization CPU metric, cache hit ratio, miss latency, and correctness regression alerts to Console dashboards
notes_and_tradeoffs: Lexeme cache semantics: we accept eventual eviction — not intended for long-term persistence. This reduces memory pressure but can cause transient misses after restarts.
Cache key must include model vocab hash to avoid cross-model tokenization mismatches (e.g., tokenizer variants, tokenizer merges). This increases cache cardinality but is safe.

We considered a global shared cache across tenants to maximize reuse but rejected it due to privacy and tenant isolation concerns; instead we design per-tenant namespacing with optional shared canonical fragments for public templates.

Fast-paths risk: ascii-only fast-path improves small prompt latency but requires careful correctness coverage for mixed-byte sequences; we will disable fast-path for inputs showing non-ascii during quick sniff.
Memory vs latency: LRU size tunes the tradeoff — we will expose configuration knobs and ship conservative defaults (128MB per runtime node) and observe in canary.
Alternative approaches like moving tokenization to an external microservice were evaluated but rejected for added network latency and complexity for small prompts.

Security: no plaintext prompt material is persisted to disk by cache; cache entries are in-memory only and tied to tenant ids. For Private deployments with stricter controls, feature will be opt-in until security review completes.
